summary: An experimental approach for using LDAP as a network information service. It maps information about TCP/IP and UNIX systems, like users, groups and hosts, into directory entries so that they can be looked up through the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol.

eli5.summary: Computers in an office need a shared list of who the users are and where machines live. This memo suggests keeping that list in a directory that everyone can ask.

subtitle: A schema for storing network and system information in LDAP directories

tldr.problem: UNIX and TCP/IP systems need to look up users, groups, hosts, and services through nameservices, traditionally using flat files or NIS; LDAP offers better scalability and extensibility, but there was no standard schema for representing these system entities in LDAP directories.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a set of LDAP object classes and attributes for representing UNIX-related entities (users, groups, hosts, services) and TCP/IP configuration data. It maps traditional nameservice lookups (like getpwnam and gethostbyname) to LDAP search filters on these classes.
tldr.outcome: Systems can replace traditional nameservices with LDAP as the primary directory service for users, groups, hosts, and services, reducing redundancy and improving scalability. The schema has been widely adopted for LDAP-based system administration.

today: RFC 2307 is an Experimental Protocol, but it achieved widespread adoption in practice. The schema became the de facto standard for LDAP-based system administration on UNIX and Linux systems. Many LDAP directory implementations (including OpenLDAP, Active Directory schema extensions, and others) adopted this schema. Today, integrating UNIX user management with LDAP is a common enterprise practice, and this RFC's object classes and attributes remain the foundation for such deployments.

sections.title: Background and Motivation
sections.content:
UNIX systems and TCP/IP networks require the ability to resolve many types of entities through nameservices. Traditional approaches include flat files (like /etc/passwd and /etc/hosts), the Network Information Service (NIS), and the Domain Name System (DNS). Each has limitations: flat files are not distributed, NIS uses flat data structures with limited extensibility, and DNS is designed primarily for host and service names, not user accounts.

LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is a distributed, hierarchical directory service protocol offering better scalability and extensibility than traditional nameservices. However, making operating systems and applications use LDAP as the primary nameservice requires a clear schema mapping system entities into X.500 directory structure. This RFC proposes such a schema, mapped from the original NIS entity types but expressed as LDAP object classes and attributes.
sections.eli5: Every computer needs to know who its users are and where other computers live. Normally this information is in different places. LDAP is a way to put all of it in one directory that many machines can ask.

sections.title: Object Classes and Attribute Schema
sections.content:
The RFC defines 13 new object classes and approximately 20 new attributes. Key object classes include posixAccount (representing a user account with POSIX attributes like UID and home directory), shadowAccount (for shadow password fields), posixGroup (representing a group), and TCP/IP-related classes like ipService, ipProtocol, ipHost, and ipNetwork.

Attributes include numeric identifiers (uidNumber, gidNumber), paths (homeDirectory, loginShell), IP information (ipHostNumber, ipNetworkNumber), and netgroup support. The RFC also defines two new syntax types: nisNetgroupTripleSyntax for NIS netgroups (host, user, domain tuples) and bootParameterSyntax for boot parameters. These structures preserve the semantics of the original flat-file and NIS entity types while mapping them to LDAP's hierarchical structure.
sections.eli5: An account object stores the user's name, ID number, home folder, and password. A host object stores the computer's name and IP address. They fit together like building blocks in the directory.

sections.title: Implementation and Lookup Methods
sections.content:
The RFC maps traditional C library functions to LDAP search filters. For example, getpwnam("lester") maps to the LDAP filter (&(objectClass=posixAccount)(uid=lester)). Similarly, gethostbyname("peg.aja.com") becomes (&(objectClass=ipHost)(cn=peg.aja.com)). This allows a directory user agent (DUA)—such as an LDAP-to-NIS gateway or an LDAP-aware C library—to transparently translate nameservice calls into LDAP queries.

For systems with multiple aliases for a single entity (such as a host with multiple DNS names), the RFC recommends using the distinguished name's RDN (relative distinguished name) as the canonical name and treating other attribute values as aliases. The schema also addresses password handling: userPassword attributes must follow a syntax like {crypt}X5/DBrWPOQQaI to indicate the hashing scheme, and the DUA selects the first matching scheme it recognizes (typically crypt for compatibility with traditional UNIX).
sections.eli5: When a program wants to know 'who is the user lester', it asks the directory: 'find me an account object where the login name is lester', and the directory replies with all the information.

sections.title: Advanced Features and Extensions
sections.content:
The schema supports sophisticated features for system administration. Shadow passwords can be represented using the shadowAccount class, which stores password aging information (last change date, minimum and maximum age, expiration) in separate attributes, allowing DUAs to implement password policies without granting access to the encrypted password itself.

The RFC also defines nisNetgroup objects to represent NIS netgroups (sets of hosts and users with domain context) and bootableDevice and ieee802Device classes for storing boot parameters and MAC addresses used in network boot scenarios. The ipService class supports multi-valued attributes: a single directory entry can represent multiple (port, protocol) pairs for one service (e.g., DNS on both TCP and UDP port 53), eliminating the need for separate entries. This flexibility allows the schema to adapt to different organizational structures and deployment models.
sections.eli5: You can store extra details like when a password expires, what machines can boot, and Ethernet addresses all in the same directory. It is flexible enough for many different setups.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Deployment
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that access to user and group entries should be granted on a discretionary basis, with special care for sensitive attributes. Encrypted passwords (which use widely-known hash functions like crypt) pose a dictionary attack risk if exposed to untrusted users; the RFC recommends that sites with strong security requirements use dedicated authentication services or restrict password access to privileged DUAs that implement shadow password service.

Administrative access control is critical: only administrators should be able to modify entries in this schema (except allowing users to change their own password), because modifying sensitive attributes like uidNumber or gidNumber could compromise system security. The RFC recommends that a DIT (Directory Information Tree) subtree to be republished by a gateway DUA should be within the same administrative domain to preserve authority. Reference implementations were available, including LDAP-to-NIS gateways and C library integrations for systems supporting the Name Service Switch (NSS) interface, with conversion tools to migrate existing flat-file data into LDAP.
sections.eli5: You must be careful about who can read and change user information, especially passwords. Only administrators should be able to change important things like ID numbers, and each person should be able to change only their own password.
